title: Neighbors and Norms
theme: Communities and society: what groups share and expect
objectives: I can describe what holds a community together using ten precise words.
I can explain the difference between a norm and a rule and give an example of each.
I can use co- and col- to work out the meaning of words about working together.
I can write about a group I belong to using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Social studies and fiction both assume students can talk about groups: who is in them, how they decide, and what they expect of one another. These ten words give students that language. Four words name how people act together (cooperate, volunteer, mutual, collective), four describe a community or its members (diverse, civic, inclusive, minority), and two name unwritten expectations (norm, ritual). The co-/col- prefix links cooperate and collective, and the word minority prepares students for later work on majority rule and the protection of rights.

words.def: Made up of many different kinds of people or things.
words.ex: The school's diverse student body includes families from more than twenty countries.
words.ex2: A diverse forest has many kinds of trees, insects, and birds.
words.nonExample: A field planted with only one kind of grass is not diverse.

apps.academic: A diverse set of sources gives a writer more than one point of view.
apps.writing: Use diverse for groups with many different kinds of members; name the kinds to be specific.

cloze.s: The city's ___ food markets sell dishes from nearly every part of the world.

cloze2.s: A ___ playlist includes classical, hip-hop, folk, and jazz.

misuse.s: The club was diverse because every member had the same background, hobby, and opinion.
misuse.why: Diverse means made up of many different kinds; everyone being the same is the opposite.

words.def: To work together toward a shared goal.
words.ex: The two classes cooperated to build a float for the parade.
words.ex2: If everyone cooperates, we can clean the whole park before lunch.
words.nonExample: Two people pulling a rope in opposite directions are not cooperating.

apps.academic: Groups that cooperate share tasks and listen to one another's ideas.
apps.spoken: Can you cooperate with me on this one?
apps.writing: Use cooperate with a person or group: cooperate with a partner.

cloze.s: The ants ___ to carry a dead beetle back to the nest, each one lifting a small part.

cloze2.s: The twins agreed to ___ and share the computer, taking turns every fifteen minutes.

misuse.s: The two teams cooperated by refusing to speak to each other and working alone.
misuse.why: To cooperate is to work together; refusing to speak and working alone is the opposite.

visual.alt: A handshake beside two puzzle pieces fitting together.

words.def: To offer to do something without being forced or paid.

senses.def: A person who works without pay by choice.
senses.example: A volunteer read stories to the children at the library.

words.ex: Dev volunteered to carry the heavy boxes to the car.
words.ex2: Hundreds of residents volunteered to plant trees along the river.
words.nonExample: A job you are ordered to do is not something you volunteer for.

apps.academic: Many museums rely on people who volunteer their time as guides.
apps.spoken: Who wants to volunteer to go first?
apps.writing: Use volunteer as a verb with to: volunteer to help, volunteer to lead.

cloze.s: When the teacher asked who could stay after school to stack chairs, three students ___.

cloze2.s: Because nobody was paid, every worker at the food drive had chosen to ___ to be there.

misuse.s: Mia volunteered to wash the dishes when her mother ordered her to do it.
misuse.why: To volunteer is to offer by choice; being ordered is not volunteering.

visual.alt: A raised hand beside a broom.

words.def: Having to do with a city, a community, or the duties of its citizens.
words.ex: Voting is a civic duty that helps shape a community.
words.ex2: The civic center hosts town meetings and art shows.
words.nonExample: A private joke between two friends is not a civic matter.

apps.academic: In civics class, students learn how local government makes decisions.
apps.spoken: Going to the town meeting is a civic thing to do.
apps.writing: Use civic with duty, pride, group, or center to name what belongs to a community.

cloze.s: Cleaning up the park together made the neighbors feel real ___ pride.

cloze2.s: A ___ leader attends town meetings and speaks up for the neighborhood.

misuse.s: It was a civic matter because it involved only one person's private diary.
misuse.why: Civic means having to do with a community; a private diary is not a community matter.

visual.alt: A town hall building beside a ballot box.

words.def: Shared or felt equally by two or more people.
words.ex: The neighbors had a mutual respect for each other's gardens.
words.ex2: It was a mutual decision: both friends agreed to end the argument.
words.nonExample: A gift that only one person enjoys is not a mutual benefit.
words.rel: felt or shared by both sides

apps.academic: Trade works best when both countries get a mutual benefit.
apps.writing: Use mutual for something two or more sides share: mutual respect, mutual friends.

cloze.s: The business partners had a ___ interest in the shop's success, since both would share the profits.

cloze2.s: Their ___ dislike of spiders made the two classmates instant friends.

misuse.s: Their mutual friendship was one-sided: only Leo cared, and Sam did not care at all.
misuse.why: Mutual means shared equally; a one-sided friendship is not mutual.

visual.alt: A handshake with arrows going in both directions.

words.def: Done or shared by a whole group together.
words.ex: The collective effort of the whole class cleaned the beach in an hour.
words.ex2: The town's collective memory of the flood still shapes its rules about building near the river.
words.nonExample: A decision made by one person alone is not collective.

apps.academic: A collective decision is one the whole group makes together.
apps.spoken: It took a collective effort to move the piano.
apps.writing: Use collective for effort, action, or ownership that belongs to a whole group.

cloze.s: The mural was a ___ project; every student in the school painted a section.

cloze2.s: When the whole neighborhood acted together, their ___ voice was loud enough for the mayor to hear.

misuse.s: A collective decision is one that a single person makes alone without asking anyone.
misuse.why: Collective means shared by a whole group; one person alone is individual.

visual.alt: A group of people painting one large mural.

words.frame: Our collective effort made it possible to ___.

words.def: Welcoming everyone and not leaving anyone out.
words.ex: The inclusive playground has ramps and swings that all children can use.
words.ex2: Our club is inclusive: anyone who loves chess is welcome, no matter their age or skill.
words.nonExample: A party where only the popular kids are invited is not inclusive.

apps.academic: An inclusive classroom gives every student a way to take part.
apps.spoken: We want the game to be inclusive.
apps.writing: Use inclusive to describe a place, rule, or plan that welcomes all kinds of people.

cloze.s: The team was ___; every student who wanted to play got a spot, whatever their skill.

cloze2.s: To make the meeting more ___, the organizers hired an interpreter so that everyone could take part.

misuse.s: The inclusive club was open to only a few chosen members and shut everybody else out.
misuse.why: Inclusive means welcoming everyone; shutting people out is the opposite.

visual.alt: A smiling face with open arms beside a rainbow.

words.frame: To make ___ more inclusive, we could ___.

words.def: A usual or expected way of behaving in a group.
words.ex: In our school, raising a hand before speaking is the norm.
words.ex2: Bowing is a polite norm in some countries, while shaking hands is the norm in others.
words.nonExample: A habit that only you follow is not a norm of the group.

apps.academic: Sociologists study the norms that guide how people act in public.
apps.spoken: Being on time is the norm around here.
apps.writing: Use norm for an unwritten expectation; a rule is written and has a consequence.

cloze.s: At the library, speaking quietly is the ___, so everyone whispers.

cloze2.s: Taking off your shoes at the door is a ___ in many homes.

misuse.s: Because arriving late is the norm in our class, the teacher is shocked whenever someone comes late.
misuse.why: A norm is what is usual; if lateness is usual, no one would be shocked by it.

visual.alt: A person holding a finger to their lips beside books.

words.def: A set of actions done in the same way each time, often with special meaning.
words.ex: Every Friday, the family's ritual is to cook pancakes together.
words.ex2: The team's pregame ritual includes a handshake line and a shared cheer.
words.nonExample: Doing something once by accident is not a ritual.

apps.academic: Rituals such as a flag salute or a graduation walk bring a group together.
apps.spoken: Our morning ritual is pancakes and music.
apps.writing: Use ritual for a repeated action that carries meaning for the people who do it.

cloze.s: Each morning, the old man followed the same ___: he watered his tomatoes, then drank tea on the porch.

cloze2.s: Lighting candles on the cake is a birthday ___ in many families.

misuse.s: The ritual changed completely every time, so nobody ever did it the same way twice.
misuse.why: A ritual is done the same way each time; changing it every time is not a ritual.

visual.alt: A birthday cake with a lit candle.

words.frame: A ritual my family has is ___.

words.def: The smaller part of a group; fewer than half of the people or votes.
words.ex: Only a minority of the class wanted pizza, so the group chose sandwiches.
words.ex2: In a fair community, the rights of a minority are protected even when the majority decides.
words.nonExample: Sixty out of one hundred voters is not a minority.
words.rel: the smaller side of a vote or group

apps.academic: Majority rule works best when the rights of the minority are protected.
apps.spoken: I was in the minority on that vote.
apps.writing: Use minority for fewer than half; the opposite is majority.

cloze.s: Only a ___ of the voters, about one in five, supported the new rule.

cloze2.s: Even when she was in the ___ at the meeting, Aisha spoke up and the group listened.

misuse.s: Ninety of the one hundred voters made up the minority.
misuse.why: A minority is fewer than half; ninety of one hundred is the majority.

passage.title: The Lot on Ellis Street
paras: The vacant lot on Ellis Street had been empty for years until Ms. Okoye began knocking on doors. Her neighbors came from many places and spoke five languages, so her idea of a community garden faced a puzzle: how could such a diverse group agree on anything? She wrote her flyers in all five languages and invited everyone to a meeting.

At the first civic meeting, held in the library basement, an interpreter sat beside every table. Ms. Okoye called it an inclusive meeting, because no one would be left out for not knowing English. The group voted on a name, a budget, and a work schedule. Most neighbors wanted vegetables. A minority, led by Mr. Tran, wanted flowers to attract bees. Instead of ignoring them, the group voted to give one corner of the garden to flowers.

Over the spring, a few norms took shape without anyone writing them down: everyone sweeps the path before leaving, tools go back on their hooks, and anyone with extra seedlings shares them. Teenagers began to volunteer on Saturdays, hauling soil and building raised beds. "None of us could do this alone," Mr. Tran said. "It takes a collective effort." Adults and students learned to cooperate, passing buckets of water in a long line.

By midsummer, the neighbors had a ritual. Every Friday at sunset they ate together at a long table, and each person brought a dish from home. The friendship was mutual: the gardeners gave away extra tomatoes, and the neighbors who did not garden brought bread, music, and stories. The vacant lot was no longer empty. It had become the place where Ellis Street gathered.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, Ms. Okoye calls the meeting "inclusive." This means the meeting was
choices: short and well organized
held in a public library
open only to people who knew English
welcoming to everyone who wanted to take part
qs.why: Interpreters at every table meant no one would be left out, which is what inclusive means.

qs.q: Why did the group give a corner of the garden to flowers?
choices: Most neighbors wanted flowers more than vegetables.
Ms. Okoye was the only person who liked vegetables.
The lot was too small for vegetables.
They wanted to include the smaller group's idea instead of ignoring it.
qs.why: The group heard the minority's idea and chose to honor it, which shows an inclusive community.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, which sentence best shows a norm?
choices: Teenagers began to volunteer on Saturdays.
Everyone sweeps the path before leaving, though no one wrote it down.
Mr. Tran said it took a collective effort.
They passed buckets of water in a long line.
qs.why: A norm is an expected way of acting that has not been written as a rule, and sweeping the path fits.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the relationship between neighbors was mutual?
choices: Gardeners gave away tomatoes, and non-gardeners brought bread, music, and stories.
Ms. Okoye wrote flyers in five languages.
The meeting was in the library basement.
Teenagers hauled soil on Saturdays.
qs.why: Mutual means shared by both sides, and each side gave something to the other.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Gardens are the best way to make friends.
Neighbors with different backgrounds can build a shared place by listening to one another and working together.
A leader should make every decision for a group.
People who speak the same language work better together.
qs.why: The story shows a diverse group planning, voting, working, and celebrating together.

argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. Volunteering can build civic ___, but a requirement might ___.

constructed.prompt: Describe one norm and one ritual in a group you belong to. Explain how they are different.

constructed.model: In my family, the norm is to put your phone away at dinner, and our ritual is that each person shares one good thing from the day. The norm tells us how to behave, but the ritual is something we do the same way every time.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that describe how communities work, using a narrative about neighbors who build a garden together. They study the prefixes co- and col- and the suffixes -ive and -ity, and they write about groups they belong to, distinguishing unwritten norms from written rules.

notes.va.diverse.adj: Diverse means many different kinds. Ask students to be specific about what kinds: backgrounds, languages, interests, plants. Students sometimes use diverse as a synonym for different; diverse needs a group.
notes.va.cooperate.v: Break into co- (together) and operate (work). Contrast with compete. Ask students to describe a time cooperation was harder than doing it alone and why it was worth it.
notes.va.volunteer.v: Volunteer is by choice. Distinguish from being asked or ordered. Note the noun use (a volunteer) as a second sense. Ask for examples of volunteering that do not involve money at all.
notes.va.civic.adj: Civic belongs to a community. Link to civics class. Students often confuse civic with civil; point out that the two are related but used differently.
notes.va.mutual.adj: Mutual is shared by both sides. Use sentences about respect, interests, and friends. Students sometimes use mutual to mean shared by many; the core idea is two or more equally.
notes.va.collective.adj: Collective is the whole group together. Link to the prefix col- (together). Contrast with individual. Ask for a collective effort at school.
notes.va.inclusive.adj: Inclusive is welcoming to everyone. Connect to include and inclusion. Ask students to design one change that makes a school event more inclusive.
notes.va.norm.n: A norm is unwritten and expected. Contrast with a rule, which is written and has a consequence. Have students list five norms in the lunchroom.
notes.va.ritual.n: A ritual is the same action done the same way with meaning. Avoid limiting to religion. Use birthdays, team handshakes, and graduation. Ask what makes an action a ritual and not just a habit.
notes.va.minority.n: Minority means fewer than half. Pair with majority. Keep the focus on votes and numbers first, then discuss why rights matter for any smaller group. Students may think minority is a label for a type of person; teach it here as a count.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says everyone sweeps the path, but no one wrote it down. That is an expected way of acting, so it is a norm, not a rule. A rule would be written and have a consequence. The word norm helps me name unwritten expectations.'
discuss: Which of these ten words describes your classroom best? Why?
How can a group stay inclusive when the majority wants something different?
misconceptions: A norm is the same as a rule.
Minority always refers to a type of person.
A ritual has to be religious.
Civic and civil mean the same thing.
extend: Interview a family member about a ritual in your family and write a short description using at least five unit words.
Write a short speech for a school meeting that uses civic, mutual, and inclusive.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the paired ideas (norm/ritual, majority/minority, cooperate/volunteer) two days later in discussion, then at one week by having students describe a group using at least five words. Connect to inhabit, prosper, surplus, and differ from earlier units.

frames: A minority of ___ wanted ___, so the group ___.
We cooperate by ___, and the result is a collective ___.
wida.oral: Partner A describes a group and one of its customs without naming the group. Partner B uses a word from the unit to name the custom and says why the group follows it.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: ofrecerse (volunteer, may be more natural as 'ofrecerse como voluntario'), cívico, mutuo, colectivo, inclusivo, norma, minoría.

Sense boundaries: volunteer taught as a verb (noun use in senses); minority taught as a count (fewer than half) and kept neutral about groups of people; norm vs. rule contrast is a classroom distinction, not a dictionary rule.
Passage is fiction; languages and demographics are invented and no real place is claimed.
